passages.happening:
The Canaanite king of Arad, in the southern desert of Canaan, hears that Israel is coming, and ‘he attacked Israel and captured some prisoners’ (verse 1).

Israel makes a vow to the LORD: “If You will deliver this people into our hands, we will devote their cities to destruction” (verse 2). God hears, and gives them the victory. “Israel devoted them and their cities to destruction; so they named the place Hormah” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 20 closed the old era with the deaths of Miriam and Aaron. Chapter 21 opens a new one. For the first time since the battle with Amalek long before, Israel wins.

The name Hormah has been heard already. A generation earlier the people went up to fight against God's command and were routed ‘all the way to Hormah’ (14:45). Now, at the same place, the result is turned round. The difference is not that Israel has grown stronger. The first time they went without God. This time they ask him first.

Notice also who began it. The king of Arad attacked and took prisoners. Israel's vow was made with its own people in an enemy's hands.

The words ‘devote to destruction’ translate the Hebrew verb charam. The name Hormah comes from it. It meant giving something wholly to God, so that the victors took nothing for themselves. In war it meant that the people of a town were killed and its goods destroyed or handed to the sanctuary. The practice was known outside Israel. The Moabite king Mesha, in an inscription of the ninth century BC, says that he did the same to an Israelite town in honor of his god Chemosh.

These three verses are the first place in Numbers where this practice appears, and they are hard to read. The last passage of this chapter takes the question up.

There is a question of history too. Digging at Tel Arad has found little or no settlement from the period to which many date the exodus. Some scholars answer that the name belonged to a different site at the time. Some prefer a different date. Some doubt the account. These notes do not settle it.
passages.later:
The book of Judges tells of a later capture of the same place and repeats the name: ‘So it was called Hormah’ (Judges 1:17).

Deuteronomy sets out the law of the ban and its stated reason, that Israel should not learn the worship of the nations of Canaan (Deuteronomy 20:16-18).
passages.asks: At Hormah a generation earlier Israel fought without asking God, and lost. Ask what you have tried a second time in the same way and with the same result. And ask what it would mean to bring it to God before you begin.

passages.happening:
Israel sets out to go around Edom, and the people grow impatient on the way (verse 4). They speak ‘against God and against Moses’: “Why have you led us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? There is no bread or water, and we detest this wretched food!” (verse 5).

“So the LORD sent venomous snakes among the people, and many of the Israelites were bitten and died” (verse 6).

The people come to Moses. “We have sinned by speaking against the LORD and against you. Intercede with the LORD so He will take the snakes away from us” (verse 7). Moses prays.

“Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘Make a fiery serpent and mount it on a pole. When anyone who is bitten looks at it, he will live.’ So Moses made a bronze snake and mounted it on a pole. If anyone who was bitten looked at the bronze snake, he would live” (verses 8-9).
passages.hearers:
This is the last of the complaint stories that began in chapter 11, and it follows their pattern: complaint, judgment, prayer, rescue. Two things are different.

The complaint goes further than before. Earlier the people spoke against Moses and Aaron. Here the text says they spoke ‘against God’. And the ‘wretched food’ they detest is the manna, the bread God had given them every morning for forty years.

The response goes further too. For the first time in these stories the people say, ‘We have sinned.’ No one has to tell them. The new generation has learned something its parents did not.

Snakes were a real danger in the deserts of the region. The word translated ‘fiery serpent’ is saraph. It probably comes from the Hebrew root for burning and describes the burning pain of the bite.

Then comes the surprising cure. The people had asked that the snakes be taken away. God does not take them away. He gives a way to live among them. And the remedy is an image of the very thing that was killing them, lifted up where everyone in the camp could see it.

It asked almost nothing of the person bitten. There was nothing to pay, nothing to prepare and nowhere to go. A dying person had only to look. The look itself was an act of trust. It meant taking God at his word that this was his remedy.

There is a play on words in the Hebrew. Snake is nachash. Bronze is nechoshet. The word nachash is also the word for the serpent in the garden in Genesis 3. The text does not draw that link out, so it should be noticed and not pressed.

Serpent images were known in the area. Excavators found a small copper snake at a shrine in the Timna valley, in the far south. In Egypt the cobra was a sign of royal and divine power, and snake images were used as charms. So an Israelite could easily have misunderstood the bronze snake as a thing with power of its own. Later that is exactly what happened.
passages.later:
Centuries afterward the bronze snake was still in Jerusalem, and people were burning incense to it. King Hezekiah destroyed it: “He also demolished the bronze snake called Nehushtan that Moses had made, for up to that time the Israelites had burned incense to it” (2 Kings 18:4). A gift of God had been turned into an idol.

Jewish teachers were careful to say that the bronze snake did not heal by itself. The Wisdom of Solomon, a Jewish book written in Greek, says that the one who turned toward it was saved not by what he saw but by God (Wisdom 16:7). The Mishnah says that Israel was healed when the people looked upward and set their hearts on their Father in heaven.

Jesus took up this story when he spoke with Nicodemus: “Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life” (John 3:14-15).
passages.hard:
How could looking at a bronze snake heal anyone? And what does Jesus mean by comparing himself to it?

On the first question the Old Testament and its Jewish readers agree. The bronze had no power. God healed. He attached his promise to an act of looking, and those who trusted the promise lived. When later generations began to honor the object itself, a faithful king broke it in pieces.

On the second question, the line from this chapter to Jesus is one the New Testament draws itself. It is in Jesus' own words in John 3:14-15. His comparison has several points, and each can be seen in this chapter. The people were dying from something they had brought on themselves. They could not cure it. God himself provided the remedy. It was lifted up in the sight of all. And it worked for anyone who looked in trust.

John's Gospel explains what ‘lifted up’ means. Jesus said, ‘And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw everyone to Myself.’ John adds, “He said this to indicate the kind of death He was going to die” (John 12:32-33). The lifting up is the cross.

There is a further likeness, which Paul's words help a reader see. The remedy in the wilderness had the shape of the thing that was killing the people. Paul writes that God sent his own Son ‘in the likeness of sinful man, as an offering for sin’ (Romans 8:3).

Jesus' use of the story does not mean that Moses or the first hearers understood it as a prediction. In its own setting it is an account of judgment and mercy in the wilderness. Jesus, reading his own Scriptures, says that the same God was about to do the same kind of thing again, once and for the whole world.

One caution belongs here. The snakes in this story were a judgment at one moment in Israel's history. The chapter gives no one reason to think that a snakebite, an illness or an accident today is a punishment from God.
passages.asks: The bitten were told to look and live. Nothing else was asked of them. Ask whether you find it hard to accept a rescue that asks nothing of you but trust. And ask what good gift of God you may have begun to treat as a thing with power of its own, as Israel later treated the bronze snake.

passages.happening:
Israel moves on by stages: Oboth, Iye-abarim, the Valley of Zered, and then across the Arnon, the river that marks the border of Moab (verses 10-13). The writer quotes a line from ‘the Book of the Wars of the LORD’ (verse 14).

At a place called Beer, which means well, God says to Moses, “Gather the people so that I may give them water” (verse 16). And Israel sings: “Spring up, O well, all of you sing to it! The princes dug the well; the nobles of the people hollowed it out with their scepters and with their staffs” (verses 17-18).

The road leads on to ‘the valley in Moab where the top of Pisgah overlooks the wasteland’ (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
These verses read like a traveler's record, a string of camping places. Many of the names cannot be placed today. The rivers can. The Zered and the Arnon run into the Dead Sea from the east. The Arnon is a deep gorge, and it was the northern border of Moab.

The Book of the Wars of the LORD is quoted here and nowhere else. It is lost. It seems to have been an old collection of poems about Israel's battles. The Bible's writers used sources, and here one of them says so.

The scene at the well is easy to pass over, and it is one of the happiest in the book. Compare it with Meribah in the last chapter. There the people had no water, quarreled, and were given water after a bitter scene. Here no one complains. God offers water before anyone asks. And the people sing.

It is the first song the story records since the song on the far shore of the sea in Exodus 15. Forty years lie between the two. The well song is short and glad. The leaders dig with their staffs of office, and the people sing to the water as it rises.

Something has changed in Israel. The same people who were bitten in the last passage are singing in this one.
passages.later:
Isaiah uses the picture of a well for the joy of being rescued by God: “With joy you will draw water from the springs of salvation” (Isaiah 12:3).

At a well in Samaria Jesus spoke of water of another kind: ‘the water I give him will become in him a fount of water springing up to eternal life’ (John 4:14).
passages.asks: At Meribah the people quarreled for water. At Beer they were given it unasked, and they sang. Ask what God has given you lately before you asked for it. And ask when you last sang, or simply gave thanks aloud, for something as ordinary as water.

passages.happening:
Israel sends messengers to Sihon, king of the Amorites, with the same request it had made to Edom: “Let us pass through your land” (verse 22). Israel will keep to the King's Highway and touch nothing.

“But Sihon would not let Israel pass through his territory. Instead, he gathered his whole army and went out to confront Israel in the wilderness” (verse 23). Israel defeats him and takes his land, from the Arnon to the Jabbok, with his city Heshbon (verses 24-26). An old song about Heshbon is quoted (verses 27-30).

Then Og, king of Bashan, comes out to battle at Edrei. God says to Moses, ‘Do not fear him, for I have delivered him into your hand’ (verse 34). “So they struck down Og, along with his sons and his whole army, until no remnant was left. And they took possession of his land” (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
The request to Sihon is word for word the request to Edom in chapter 20: safe passage on the main road, with nothing taken. When Edom refused, Israel walked away. When Sihon refuses, he does more. He marches out with his whole army to attack. The battle is fought because he brings it.

The land in question lies east of the Jordan. Heshbon, Dibon and Medeba are towns on the high plain north of the Arnon. Several of these names appear on the Mesha inscription, found in 1868 at Dhiban, the ancient Dibon. Bashan lay further north.

The poem in verses 27 to 30 is a taunt song. It remembers that Sihon had himself taken this land from Moab by war. Now it has been taken from him in turn. Chemosh, named in verse 29, was the god of Moab.

Here too there are questions of history. Digging at sites proposed for Heshbon has found little from the period to which many date these events. Scholars answer in the same range of ways as for Arad, and these notes do not settle it.

These two victories gave Israel its first territory. They were remembered in Israel's worship for centuries. And they set up the next story. The king of Moab has watched what happened to his neighbors, and he is afraid.
passages.later:
Psalm 136 sings of both kings in its long thanksgiving: ‘Sihon king of the Amorites’ and ‘Og king of Bashan’, each line answered with “His loving devotion endures forever” (Psalm 136:19-20).

Deuteronomy retells the story and adds that Israel first sent Sihon ‘an offer of peace’ (Deuteronomy 2:26).

The New Testament turns the church's fight in another direction: “For our struggle is not against flesh and blood” (Ephesians 6:12).
passages.hard:
How should a reader understand the destruction of the towns of Arad and the killing of the peoples of Sihon and Og?

These are among the hardest passages in the Old Testament, and they belong with the wider question of the conquest. Christians who receive these books as God's word read them in more than one way.

Some take the accounts as they stand. On this reading God, who gives every life, judged particular nations whose wickedness had become complete. God had told Abraham centuries before that his descendants would wait, ‘for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete’ (Genesis 15:16). This happened at one point in history and was never given as a general rule.

Others note that ancient reports of war, the Mesha inscription among them, used sweeping language of total destruction as an ordinary way of describing a victory. On this reading the words may not be meant as a count of every person killed.

Others read these passages as showing the limits of Israel's moral understanding at the time, later corrected by the fuller knowledge of God in Christ. Those who reject this reading say that it weakens the authority of Scripture.

Each reading has a cost, and these notes take no side. Several things can be said on any of them. The Bible does not offer these wars as a pattern for later believers. Israel itself is judged in this same chapter, by the snakes. The wars with Sihon and Og began when those kings marched out to attack. And the New Testament tells God's people that their fight is not against flesh and blood.

No one may use these verses as a reason for violence against any person or people. They name kingdoms that passed away long ago, and they say nothing about any nation or conflict today.

A reader who finds these verses troubling is in good company. The site's pages on the violence of the Old Testament and on the command to destroy the Canaanites go further.
passages.asks: Israel asked for a road and was met with an army. Ask how you respond when a fair request is answered with hostility. And ask what you do with the pages of the Bible that trouble you most: whether you have ever stayed with one long enough to say honestly what troubles you about it.
